analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent several temporary tax cuts, including full estate tax repeal and a larger child credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee: it was referred there the day it was introduced on January 11, 2007, and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Several tax cuts from the 2001 Bush tax law were temporary, set to expire after 2010. This bill would have written them permanently into the tax code: the deduction for state and local sales taxes (mainly helping people in states without an income tax), the expanded child credit, relief from the marriage penalty, the tuition deduction, the small deduction for teachers' classroom expenses, and full repeal of the estate tax. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, middle-income families would have kept a larger child credit and marriage penalty relief permanently, taxpayers in states without an income tax (like Florida and Texas) would have kept deducting their sales taxes, and students and families would have kept a deduction of up to $4,000 for tuition. The single largest permanent gain, however, would have gone to heirs of very large estates, since the estate tax would have been repealed outright rather than phased down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle-income families and heirs of large estates

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the expanded child tax credit and marriage penalty relief, which primarily benefit families with children and married two-earner couples.
Makes permanent the deduction for state and local sales taxes, which mainly helps taxpayers in states that rely on sales taxes instead of income taxes.

Makes permanent the deduction for up to $4,000 in tuition and related higher-education expenses, and the small deduction for elementary and secondary school teachers' out-of-pocket classroom expenses.
Exempts the 2001 law's estate tax repeal from its December 31, 2010 sunset, permanently eliminating the federal estate tax rather than letting the scheduled phase-down stand.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. None of the provisions had offsets, so the forgone revenue would have been borrowed or made up later through other taxes and cuts. Within the package, the estate tax repeal concentrates its benefits on heirs of the largest estates, while the cost of lost revenue is spread across all future taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no revenue offsets, so making all the provisions permanent would have added substantially to federal deficits and national debt.

Full, permanent repeal of the estate tax would deliver the largest benefits to a small group — heirs of the wealthiest estates — while permanently giving up a tax that applies only to very large inheritances.
Bundling popular middle-class provisions with estate tax repeal made the package all-or-nothing, leaving no room to make the family and education provisions permanent on their own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The middle-class provisions — child credit, marriage penalty relief, tuition and sales tax deductions — are broadly popular and would have removed annual uncertainty for families. But the bill tied them to permanent full estate tax repeal and offered no way to pay for any of it, so its long-term cost in borrowing and lost revenue was large and skewed toward the wealthiest households.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart introduced the bill on January 11, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Sixty-nine House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats did.
The committee took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 2001 law's scheduled phase-down of the estate tax stayed in place, so the federal estate tax was not permanently repealed and the Treasury kept that revenue; the middle-class tax provisions in the bill continued only as repeatedly renewed temporary measures, which Congress handled through other bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue; estate tax stayed in place

for.name: 69 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 69 cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill, so support was entirely from one party while the other controlled its fate.

industries.note: Full estate tax repeal would permanently eliminate a tax owed only by very large estates, a direct gain concentrated on the richest families, with the revenue given up instead borne by future taxpayers through borrowing.
Permanent child credit and marriage penalty relief would deliver a steady, predictable tax cut to working families with children.

industries.industry: Taxpayers in states without an income tax
industries.note: The sales tax deduction, which mainly benefits residents of states like Florida and Texas, would have become permanent rather than requiring periodic renewal.
The tuition deduction of up to $4,000 would have been locked in instead of lapsing.
